en: Homage to the Buddha!

One should suppress Kaliṅga with *oṃ āḥ hūṃ*, which serves as the basis for the arising of the Lord of Three Syllables; he is known as the Vajra of Body, Speech, and Mind in the ultimate sense (*paramārthakāya*).
*Ehi vatsa mahāyānaṃ mantracāryanayaṃ vidhim*.

"I shall teach you correctly, for you are a vessel for the Great Way (Mahāyāna). I shall teach you the ritual method of the Mantra-Practice Way; that which is the Mantra Way is indeed the Mahāyāna, its name being the 'Great Path. I shall teach you correctly—I shall instruct and reveal it to you—because you are a vessel for the Great Way, meaning that you have become a worthy recipient to be taught the Dharma of the Mantra Way.
For those who were the Perfectly Awakened Ones of the past, and likewise those yet to come..."
And those Protectors who exist in the present, abiding for the welfare of the world.

Ka: Lord Buddha of the past—those who have already attained perfect enlightenment (abhisambuddha) in former times, namely: Lord Vipaśyin, Viśvabhū, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, Kāśyapa; these are all the names of the Buddhas of the past. Tathā caivāpy anāgatāḥ: Furthermore, Lord Buddha of the future—those who are currently facing the attainment of perfect enlightenment, namely: Lord Ārya Maitreya and others, up to Samantabhadra; these are all the names of the Buddhas of the future. Pratyutpannāś ca ye nāthāḥ: And those Lords of the present—namely Lord Śrī Śākyamuni, who is called the Buddha of the present; he is the Buddha of this very time, whose teaching remains fresh in our hearts. Tiṣṭhanti ca jagaddhitāḥ: They remain for the welfare of the world; they shine forth for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings, so that the entire realm may be liberated from *saṃsāra*, and so that the world may not tremble before the fire of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*).
And by all of them, having understood this vajra and attained the supreme mantra-ritual,
the heroes reached omniscience at the foot of the Bodhi tree, which is indeed without marks.

Ka: Who is the Lord called the Buddha? He is the one who exists in the past, future, and present. There is no other path for him than that which is followed by the Buddha. "Having known the supreme ritual of mantra"—this is the Great Vehicle, the Great Path, which was practiced by him as his path leading to the City of Nirvāṇa. [a10] "The Heroes attained omniscience at the foot of the Bodhi tree, which is without characteristics. This is the reason why the method of mantra was proclaimed; it is the cause for attaining omniscience, and it is the reason they obtained the state of Buddhahood at the foot of the Bodhi tree.

The incomparable application of mantra by which the protector Śākyasiṃha shattered the great and most terrible army of Māra. O Lord, the venerable Śrī Tākyamuni, having conquered Māra, overcame all those obstacles of Māra: the Māra of afflictions (*kleśamāra*), the Māra of the aggregates (*skandhamāra*), the Māra of death (*mṛtyumāra*), and the Māra of the son of a god (*devaputramāra*). All of these were overcome by the Lord through the cause of his clarity in overcoming Māra, by means of the radiance, power, majesty, and the force of the divine *samādhi* and the practice of the method of mantra (*mantranaya*).
Therefore, apply this mind to the news for the sake of attaining omniscience;
O you of noble disposition, listen constantly, having properly withdrawn all conceptual constructions.

Ka: "O Mataṅgyan, grant [this] for the attainment of omniscience (*sarvajñātā*). Do not be hesitant regarding these sacred mantras; listen well to what the sacred mantras say, so that you may obtain all that is desired from them. 'GṚṆABHADRĀŚAYAN NITYAM': I have repeatedly instructed you on this matter; do not doubt my words. 'SAMYAK SAṄHṚTYA KALPANĀḤ': apply the intellect free from conceptualization (*nirvikalpaka*), eliminate the delusion of dogmatic attachment (*abhiniveśa*), and be at peace—do not have any doubt."
This is the excellent, glorious path of the Mahāyāna, the great manifestation,
by which you, proceeding along it, shall become Tathāgatas.

Kaḥ: Indeed, this Great Vehicle, the Great Path, has been shown to me by you. Listen well to it: *Mahāyāna Mahodayaḥ*. This is the true path leading to both heaven (*svarga*) and liberation (*apavarga*), which is capable of bestowing the great prosperity (*mahodaya*). *Mahodaya* refers to external and internal happiness: namely, excellence, wealth, power, sovereignty, and universal rule. Internal happiness is supramundane happiness, which is free from suffering, free from old age and death, and untainted by aging, illness, or death. It is the unsurpassed, noble, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), the happiness of liberation (*mokṣa*). Both external and internal happiness constitute that great prosperity (*mahodaya*) which is to be attained through the Great Vehicle, the Great Path, when it is practiced. "By means of this, you shall go," for thereafter you will be able to enjoy this Great Vehicle; "you shall become Tathāgatas," meaning you will certainly attain the state of the Buddhas. You shall directly realize the state of liberation, having acquired the two accumulations: the accumulation of knowledge (*jñāna-sambhāra*) and the accumulation of merit (*puṇya-sambhāra*). Thus it was obtained by him.
The self-existent ones (svayambhuva) are highly fortunate and worthy of sacrifice by all the world;
they have transcended existence and non-existence, being as stainless as space.

What are the limbs of that space? It is of a stainless nature, without characteristics (alakṣaṇa), without substantiality (avastuka); it cannot be grasped, it is neither above nor below, neither limited nor infinite, neither black nor white; it pervades the ten directions—such is its description.
Profound and exceedingly profound, inconceivable and untroubled, free from all conceptual proliferation, yet manifested through conceptual proliferations.

Ka: O you who possess the great, profound cave! Truly, the venerable Mahāyāna is the Great Path. It is *gambhīrātigambhīra*: [a12] deep beyond depth; *apy atarkyaṃ*: that which cannot be conceptualized, for it would be an error to attempt to do so; *anāvilaṃ*: free from defect; *sarvaprapañcarahitaṃ*: devoid of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), as well as the afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*)—namely, intoxication, hypocrisy, greed, delusion, passion, and darkness—none of these exist within it. It is truly such that it cannot be described in that way, for it is *prapañcebhyaḥ prapañcitaṃ*: made manifest by means of conceptual proliferations, since passion, hatred, and delusion are the very nature of those proliferations.
Free from action and its performance, not dependent on the two truths, this most excellent and supreme vehicle is practiced by those established in the [Madhyamaka] method.

It is without boundaries; it has no boundaries made by anyone, for it is their very nature. SATYADVAYAṂ: that which constitutes the two truths (satyadvaya) is *saṃvṛtisatya* (conventional truth) and *paramārthasatya* (ultimate truth); these are what constitute its form. [b12] ANĀŚRAYAṂ: there is no basis, neither conventional truth nor ultimate truth, in its essence. IDAṂ YĀNAVARAṂ ŚREṢṬAṂ: this is the most excellent and supreme vehicle; it is what is called Mahāyāna, the Great Path, which leads to both heaven (*svarga*) and liberation (*apavarga*). ABHYASYATA NAYE STHITĀḤ: those who abide in this method are those who practice the profound path of the Mahāyāna, the way of the sacred mantras.

OṂ! VAJRODAKA OṂ ĀḤ HŪṂ! These two are the heart-mantra of the oath. THIS IS THE WATER OF HELL FOR YOU; IT FLOWS IF THERE IS A TRANSGRESSION OF THE SAMAYA, BUT FROM GUARDING THE SAMAYA, THERE IS ACCOMPLISHMENT. MAY THE VAJRA-AMṚTA WATER BE ACCOMPLISHED!

Ka: "Weigh your mind. What is the vajra-water? This vajra-water is not like ordinary water; it is more terrible than hell. *Samayātikramo vahet*: it brings about the path of suffering, one falls away from one's family, lineage, and vehicle; that is what is meant by violating the *samaya*. At another time, it becomes a wife or a husband to the venerable Vajrajñāna. Through the protection of the *samaya*, there is success (*siddhi*); otherwise, even with great effort, if one does not guard the *samaya*, the path of the auspicious and perfected state cannot be attained by them. *Siddhaṃ vajrānṛtodakam*: in brief, this vajra-water is both poison and nectar; depending on how it is used, one attains either happiness or suffering. If you are negligent, you will encounter suffering; but if you exert effort, the auspicious and perfected state of bliss will be attained in due course. Thus he spoke.

One who possesses the vajra, the bell, and the mudrā should address that person presiding over the maṇḍala; however, a person who lacks faith and remains in the company of worldly distractions shall laugh [at him].

Do not teach the *saṅ hyaṅ vajra-ghaṇṭā-mudrā* to a person who has not seen the *maṇḍala*, nor to one who is merely a *sāmayika* (bound by convention) but lacks the secret [initiation]. Do not reveal it to such a person, even if they have received the oral instruction (*upadeśa*), for they are "one who possesses no faith" (*aśraddhavān eva*), or perhaps one who is "doubtful" (*guyuguyunta*) because they do not understand its meaning, or one who does not strive to maintain the vows of the Lord (*brata bhaṭāra*). Do not act in such a way, lest the person mock the Noble Path (*saṅ hyaṅ mārgga*). Such a person remains "staying in the company of the worldly" (*janaḥ saṅganikāsthitaḥ*); let such a person remain so, for they wander in *saṃsāra* forever. Therefore, do not lack sincere devotion (*adhimukti*) toward the Noble Vajra-Knowledge (*saṅ hyaṅ vajrajñāna*); exert yourself, O Noble One, in the observance of the *samaya*.
"This is your pledge (samaya), O Vajrī, known as Vajrasattva.
By that very [pledge], may he cause you to enter into unsurpassed vajra-knowledge. Ka:

"The sacred pledge (saṅ hyaṅ samaya) is what is called Lord Vajrasattva; 'may he cause you to enter into unsurpassed vajra-knowledge' means that he is now your heart, for this vajra-knowledge is your heart, which is to say, it is your very essence."

OṂ VAJRASATTVAḤ SVAYAM TE 'DYA CAKṢŪDGHĀṬANATATPARAḤ | UDGHĀṬAYATI SARVAKṢO VAJRACAKṢUR ANUTTARAM || "O Lord Śrī Vajrasattva, you yourself are now intent upon opening my eyes; you open all my eyes with the unsurpassed Vajra-eye. The meaning is: "O Lord Śrī Vajrasattva, you yourself are now intent upon opening my eyes"—this means that you are looking at me. "You open all my eyes with the unsurpassed Vajra-eye"—this means that you cause me to behold the venerable Maṇḍala.
Behold this maṇḍala and now generate faith;
you are born into the family of the Buddhas and are empowered by all mantras.

"O noble Maṇḍala, generate faith now!"—thus one should cause faith to arise; do not be without reverence toward the noble Maṇḍala. "You have been born [into the lineage] of the Buddhas," for you belong to the Buddha-family (*buddhakula*); for the Lord Buddha is indeed your master. "Empowered by all mantras"—this empowerment has already been performed by all the Tathāgatas, and it is consecrated by all mantras.
"All perfections are present, and these are for the sake of the yoga of accomplishment."
Protect the pledge for the sake of accomplishment; be diligent in the mantras.

Ka: "What else is beautiful for you? Siddhayoga tayaścate—[it is] that all forms of perfection (*siddhi*) are facing you; strive to attain them! Pālaya samayaṃ siddhye—quickly practice the sacred rules (*samaya*), so that you may meet with those perfections when your time has come! Mantreṣūdyogavān bhava—be diligent in mantras, exerting enthusiasm in mantra recitation (*japa*) and worship (*pūjā*) until [the goal is reached]; do not be lazy, lest you fail to obtain the state of bliss in this very life or in a future one."
IṂ OṂ VAJRANETRĀYA, remove, remove the veil from the heart; O child, the veil of ignorance shall be removed from you by the Victors,
the supreme Kings of Physicians, with their probes, just as darkness is removed from the world by light.

O Kaliṅga: you shall experience well-being; the veil of ignorance (*ajñānapaṭala*) has vanished from your heart. You have been healed by the Lord Śrī Bajradhara Śalakair Vaidyarājendra, just as darkness is dispelled from the world by light. For example, when a person is afflicted by disease, they do not recover until they have been treated by a physician who administers medicine; once they have recovered, their health remains until finally that affliction of blindness and other ailments vanishes. In the same way, this veil of ignorance has completely vanished and is gone without remainder, having already been healed by the Lord. Therefore, you should feel at ease; do not have any doubt.
Phenomena are like reflections; they are exceedingly pure, stainless, ungraspable, and inexpressible, yet they arise from causes and karma.

Ka: "The Lord bestows the eradication of all phenomena (*sarvadharmma*), for there is no reality in them other than illusion (*māyā*) within the mirror of consciousness. Indeed, the form of that illusion within the mirror is not something produced by a creator, because its intrinsic nature (*tattva*) does not exist. Such is the case with all things (*sarvabhāva*); moreover, human birth is caused by karma which manifests here, therefore it is like a mere appearance, yet there is no solid substance. "Knowing thus these phenomena to be devoid of self-nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) and insubstantial (*svanāvilān*)."
Perform incomparable benefit for sentient beings, for you have been born as a true son of the Protectors.

[Know that] all phenomena are like an illusion; they are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) and possess various diversities. Do not be deluded by this lack of intrinsic nature regarding all phenomena. Perform incomparable benefit for sentient beings, for you are intent upon the welfare of others; you have been born as a true son of the Protectors, for you are indeed the "son of the Victor" (*jinorasa*). Therefore, do not fail to exert yourself in virtuous deeds and in the service of others.
"O child, Vajrasattva himself—the lord of all Buddhas—dwells in your heart; he is by his very nature pure, stainless, and self-arisen."

Ka: This is the gift for you: Lord Vajrasattva resides within your heart, Lord Vajrasattva who is his very essence. *Accāśuddha hy anāvilaḥ* (Extremely pure and stainless); he is of pure intrinsic nature (*śuddhasvabhāva*), for there is no passion (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), or delusion (*moha*) in him. Moreover, he is the principal among all the Tathāgatas; he is thus your very heart, the path of merit. [b16] The equipment of gnosis (*jñānasambhāra*) is obtained by him for his own sake; do not have any doubt. "From this day forward, O Protector, turn the wheel for the world."
"Fill everywhere with the stainless, supreme Dharma-conch.

Turn the wheel of those who protect [beings], O Lord Śrī Bhajradhara, for the sake of all sentient beings. Fill everywhere with the stainless, supreme Dharma-conch; furthermore, blow it so that its sound reaches the ten directions throughout the entirety of the infinite world-systems, for this Dharma-conch is one and the same as them all. "You should have no doubt in this matter; do so with a mind free from hesitation."
"Reveal the supreme, great, and peerless system of the Mantracārya.
Do not have any doubt; with a mind free from hesitation, reveal the supreme, great, and peerless system of the Mantracārya, and demonstrate this very path of the Mahāyāna Mantra.
One who acts thus is proclaimed as one who knows the debt of gratitude toward the Buddhas and is a benefactor."
And all those Vajradharas shall protect you in every way.

Ka: "O person, just as you have already been refined by the Lord, performing special worship to the Lord Buddha—this is called *upakārī* (one who has rendered service)—and since he has indeed already provided such service, the Lord is the name for such a person. 'And all those who hold the Vajra shall protect you in every way. Because he is one who has rendered service to you, and because of his compassion, that is the reason why you must strive to protect yourself day and night, inside and out, everywhere and in every direction. You must be made an object of their effort so that they may provide service to you; therefore, do not be despondent, for there is the Lord Śrī Vajrasattva who protects you as your very self."
There is nothing that cannot be accomplished through wisdom and skillful means;
having always become free from doubt with such a mind, enjoy the fivefold objects of desire.

Ka: "There is no activity that you cannot perform; for even if the three worlds are filled with difficult deeds, there is nothing that cannot be done by one who dwells in the heavens, the human realm, or the underworld. Such exceedingly difficult karma can be performed by you. With wisdom and skillful means as your mind (*prajñopāyena cetasā*), yet making wisdom your guide (*prajñāmatā*), being always free from fear (*nirviśaṅkaḥ sadābhūtvā*), and never letting go of your mind that is forever free of doubt; enjoy the five objects of desire (*prabhuṅkṣva kāmapañcakam*). You may enjoy all the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*), all varieties of sense objects (*sarvaviṣaya*); do not reject any of them for enjoyment, for you are a practitioner (*sādhaka*). Yet, do not fail to take hold of that state of being free from doubt."

For just as Bodhisattvas guard the Vinaya through their realization, so too should one act for the benefit of all sentient beings while remaining pure despite passion and the other afflictions. What are the limbs of the Lord Siksa Bodhisattva Mahāsattva? They are the following: he is one who has mastered the noble method of mantra (*mantranaya*). "Mastered" (*amběk temen*) means: acting for the sake of others, being free from the conceptualization of the afflictions (*kleśa*), and being untainted by passion, hatred, and delusion (*rāga-dveṣa-moha*).
Furthermore, those others who are hostile to the samaya, those people who have fallen from the samaya, and those who are to be slain—
these must be dealt with with effort for the sake of protecting the Buddha’s teaching.

There are people who hate the *saṃhita* of the Holy One and are hostile toward the *mantranaya* of the Holy One; "those people who have fallen from their *samaya*. There are people who have fallen from their *samaya*, having already completed the *samaya* and received the oral instructions (*upadeśa*). What then will be their end? How is it that they are dealt with? The Guru explains this: "They are to be killed with effort. Such people as those who hate the *samaya* and have fallen from the *samaya* must be executed; they are not spared by the Lord. "In order to protect the teaching of the Buddha"—that is, for the sake of guarding the teaching of the Lord, the Holy Buddha, and for the preservation of the *samaya* of the Holy One—such is the result of being hostile toward the *samaya* and so forth.
It has been seen; you have entered the supreme secret *maṇḍala*.
Freed from all sins, you have become purified this very day.

Having drunk the *tāmbūla* of the *ka-paka* (the *ka* syllable), you have now entered the *maṇḍala* of the Lord (*saṅ hyaṅ*) who is the ultimate secret. Furthermore, they have offered the *vulatta* (betel) to the Lord of the *maṇḍala*.

"Completely liberated from all sins; having entered this maṇḍala and been instructed in its profound secret, the reason why all your sins have vanished is that they have disappeared as if washed away, vanished root and branch. You are now indeed purified. Be at ease, do not have any doubt.
There is no further delight for you than this great bliss (*mahāsukha*). You are invincible and beyond reproach; rejoice, free from fear."

"O you who have returned from this Great Bliss! You have become like people who have strayed from the path of the divine Mantra-weapon; you are neither worthy of praise nor worthy of veneration. However, if you apply yourselves with effort to the practice of the divine Mantra, you shall attain the auspicious state of perfection, which cannot be seized by Māra, Tīrthikas, and the like. Rejoice, free from all fear! Therefore, be joyful; do not be timid, but offer your sincere devotion to the divine Mantra."
This *sambara* of the perfected ones' pledge must be constantly protected by you;
it is declared to be equal to all the Buddhas. Fulfill this eternal command!

Ka: With effort, guard the secret of the *sāmayika* (initiate). Do not reveal the secret of his *kuṇḍala* to others; know well those who are worthy to be taught the secret of the *sāmayika*. Do not disregard their intentions, their conduct, their actions, or their boundaries. However, if they possess sincere faith, they shall be indestructible and unbreakable regarding the *mantra* of the Lord. Therefore, you must be cautious regarding the secret of the Lord; do not have doubt, and do not be hesitant when teaching it.

Indeed, the venerable *samaya* is the limb of beings possessed of resolute faith; it is declared to be equal to all Buddhas. Now that you have received the authorization (*kṛtānujñāta*) from those All-Tathāgatas, may the Lord rejoice and accept this venerable *samaya*: "Fulfill the command eternally! You have indeed been authorized by the Lord; may all the rites of the All-Tathāgatas be successfully accomplished. "One must never abandon the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), for by the mere production of its seal (*mudrā*) as a vajra, one is undoubtedly a Buddha."

*Ka:* "The noble *bodhicitta* is that which bestows the sign (*liṅga*). *Boddhicitta ṅa:* "By means of the seal (*mudrā*) called *yad vajram iti*. The noble *vajra* is what is termed *bodhicitta*, whereas the noble *mudrā* is its ancient name. *Yasyotpādaikamātreṇa*: "By the mere arising of this," for that reason the noble *vajra* and the *mudrā*—*buddha eva na saṃśayaḥ*: "He is indeed the Buddha, without doubt"—you have spoken of the noble Buddha; you have directly realized that which was bestowed upon you. Furthermore, there is effort toward the noble *vajra*, *ghaṇṭā*, and *mudrā*.
The True Dharma is never to be rejected nor ever abandoned;
however, if one fails to explain it due to ignorance or delusion, that is not [the fault of the Dharma].

"Ka: That which is equal to the venerable True Dharma (saddharma) must never be abandoned. Furthermore, one should not disparage it, whether out of ignorance or delusion; for if one does so, one will not truly explain it. Therefore, do not act in such a way as to cause others to reject the venerable True Dharma through ignorance and delusion. This is because those people who follow the Mahāyāna are afraid when they hear the rejection of the venerable Sūtrāntas. Abandoning oneself, one should not excessively torment oneself with austerities."

"One should maintain happiness at ease; this one shall become a perfectly awakened Buddha in the future. (a21) *Pratiwārikāwakta*: "Having spoken thus, being indifferent to one's own body, and having no craving for oneself, one should not torment oneself with austerities (*tapas*). One should not be distressed by ascetic practices, nor should one cause them to become a source of suffering. "One should maintain happiness at ease" (*yathāsukhaṃ sukhaṃ dhāryam*): practice the path of the Buddha according to what is comfortable. "This one shall become a perfectly awakened Buddha in the future" (*sambuddheyam anāgataḥ*): do not fear that you will not become a Buddha. "Never abandoning the vajra, the bell, and the mudrā."

The Ācārya must not be despised, for he is equal to all the Buddhas. He who does not place the *saṅ hyaṅ vajra*, the *ghaṇṭā*, and the *mudrā* upon his head—whether at the beginning, the end, or in between—is an Ācārya who must not be despised. Furthermore, one should never commit the offense of slandering the Guru; it is not fitting for a person to show contempt toward the Ācārya, and therefore one must not hold him in low esteem. He is equal to all the Buddhas; he is equal to all the Buddhas, even as Lord Buddha himself.

And whoever would despise the teacher, who is equal to all Buddhas and is the Guru, shall always experience suffering through that contempt for all Buddhas. Who is this person? One who is arrogant, disrespectful, and does not honor the Guru, he shall always experience suffering. He returns to hell, falling into the pit of Yama, becoming the fuel for the fire of the copper-faced beast; such is the sin of a person who is arrogant toward the Guru.

Therefore, with every effort, one must never despise the Vajrācārya, the great Guru, who is a hidden and excellent holy being (*pracchannavarakalyāṇa*). [Commentary]: One must exert effort toward the Guru even if he is a "hidden and excellent holy being" (*pracchannavarakalyāṇa*), meaning that although his virtues may not be manifest, he is nonetheless such a person. Furthermore, one must "never despise him" (*nāvamanyet kadācana*); do not hold contempt for him, for not honoring the Guru is a great sin and a source of great suffering. Therefore, one should always be diligent in serving the activities of the Guru.
One's own commitment must be maintained constantly; likewise, the Tathāgata must be worshipped constantly;
and the guru’s instruction must be followed constantly, for he is equal to all the Buddhas.

Ka: Do not harbor ill-will toward the venerable Samaya; "NITYAṂ PŪJYAS TATHĀGATAḤ"—you must constantly perform worship of the Tathāgata. Lāwan: "ŚĀŚWATAṂ KṚTYAṂ TATHĀGATAPŪJĀ"—you must perpetually carry out the worship of the Tathāgata. NITYAÑ CA GURUVAIDHEYAṂ—"And always being obedient to the Guru"—you must constantly practice service to the Guru, even when the Guru is inactive. SARBVABUDDHASAMO HY ASAU—"For he is equal to all the Buddhas"—this means that the Guru is equal to all the Tathāgatas; therefore, you must serve him with obedience. DATTESMIN SARBVABUDDHEBHYO DATTAM BHAVATI CĀKṢAYAM—"What is given to him is as if given to all the Buddhas, and it becomes inexhaustible."
From that giving arises the accumulation of merit; from that accumulation comes supreme accomplishment.

[b22] Ka: "O person like you, who has performed service to the teacher (*guruśuśrūṣā*) and offered gifts and so forth to the venerable teacher—that indeed is the accumulation of the gift-store (*dānasambhāra*) toward the Lord Buddha, known as *taddānāt puṇyasambhāraḥ*. Through that connection, the store of merit (*puṇyasambhāra*) is attained; from the store comes supreme accomplishment (*sambhārāt siddhir uttamā*). Upon obtaining that store of merit, the state of perfection (*kasiddhi*) will become easily accessible to you through your effort in serving the teacher."
One should always honor one's own spiritual teacher with even one's own life-breaths,
let alone with sons, wives, or unstable wealth which should never be given away.

But one should offer even one’s own body to the venerable Guru, performing service for his sake, whether with one’s wife and children (*adeyaiḥ putradāraiḥ vā*). Let it be that one offers all one’s children to the Guru; being like slaves (*dāsabhūtāḥ*), they are the instruments for him to perform his work. How much more so with unstable riches? Do not mention what is called "wealth"—for example, gold, jewels, clothing, and silver—all of these should be offered to the venerable Guru.
For this is always extremely difficult to obtain, even in tens of millions of countless eons (*kalpāsaṃkhyeyakoṭibhiḥ*).
It bestows Buddhahood upon one who possesses diligence even in this very life.

Ka: Regarding the attainment of Buddhahood, which is extremely and supremely difficult to obtain—even if one were to spend countless millions of *kalpa*s cultivating roots of merit such as the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) until Buddhahood is reached—it is not certain that it will be attained, because of the difficulty of attaining liberation. "Buddhahood grants itself even in this very life to one who exerts effort. This Buddhahood is bestowed by the venerable Guru right here in this present birth; therefore, you must receive his grace. For this reason, it is not obstructed, nor hindered, nor delayed, nor lost, so that you may worship him with your whole being, both yourself and your children, toward that venerable Guru.
Today your birth has become fruitful, for He is well-established within you; for today you have been born as self-existent deities, equal indeed to the gods.

Today your birth has become fruitful, for He is well-established within you: O refuge of the unripened, you have truly attained the state of the Buddha; for today you have been born as self-existent deities, equal indeed to the gods—He, the Buddha, has now entered your very palms, residing there like a flower held in a closed fist.

"Venerable ones, you have been consecrated today by all the Buddhas and all the Vajrins as sovereign kings in the great kingdom of the three realms. Ka: "The meaning is that you have already been consecrated by all the Tathāgatas and all the Tathāgatīs. The name of this consecration bestowed upon you is called the *cakravarty-abhiṣeka* (the universal monarch consecration)."
"Today, having completely conquered Māra, you have entered the supreme city;
you have attained Buddhahood this very day—of this there is no doubt. [Commentary:

"Having completely conquered Māra" means that you have cast off the activities of Māra. "Entered the supreme city" means that you have certainly reached the city of Nirvāṇa right now. "Attained Buddhahood this very day" means that you have certainly achieved liberation in this very life. "By you, there is no doubt here": believe this with certainty; do not harbor any doubt.
Thus, with a serene mind, take refuge in the vajra of your own illusory nature, which bestows the bliss of the exhaustion of space;
for in this world, it is a light happiness, and you shall become equal to all Buddhas, attaining the state of eternity.

Thus he spoke: "Listen with true devotion and fix your minds upon it! Worship that which is one’s own nature (*svasamāya*), which bestows the bliss of the destruction of suffering. You must guard the sacred pledge (*samaya*) with great care, so that you may attain unsurpassed bliss. O you who are equal to all Buddhas, may you reach the state of eternity in this world, for human birth is a rare occasion for happiness. Just as others may attain the state of Buddhahood after a long time following all the Tathāgatas, therefore you must quickly practice the sacred pledge and cultivate the Great Vehicle of Mantra-naya. Do not be negligent; strive with constant effort so that the attainment of *siddhi* may be easily reached by you."
Thus ends the venerable Mahāyāna Mantranaya.
Iṃ! Homage to the Buddha! Iṃ!

Herein lies the venerable Mahāyāna teaching which I shall bestow upon you, O son of the Jinas belonging to the Tathāgata family, you who are a practitioner of the Mahāyāna; this indeed is the venerable Mahāyāna which I shall bestow upon you.

Furthermore, whether it be a mountain cave, a house, a seashore, a hut, a monastery, or a village dwelling; or if you are in a field, a grove, or any such place—O Holy One, O Protector, may that be auspicious for you. May that empty dwelling be suitable for your practice, your worship, and your rest; may there be beds, pillows, mats, and coverlets, as well as whatever else is necessary for your comfort.

Do not let your body be worn out by constant toil; rather, enjoy all these pleasures so that happiness may be yours. As for the food you eat, it will surely be digested again; therefore, do not worry about eating. Do not forget your daily devotions and circumambulations.

Thus, even though there is suffering in the body, it is no fault of yours that you seek to heal it; it is the same for you as it is for others. Do not be deceitful, for those who are truly deceitful are many. In brief: let your body indeed be well, for a healthy body is the cause of the attainment of happiness, and happiness is the cause of the attainment of a tranquil mind; a tranquil mind is the cause of the arising of *samādhi*, and *samādhi* is the cause of the attainment of liberation.

May your body be long-lived! May you have excellent clothing, fine sandals, and robes with all their proper accoutrements; may you have a water vessel of white stone, and a tooth-stick of *kekari* wood. If you are a Buddha-ṛṣi, may you have a water jar, a sitting mat, and ashes, sandalwood, and seeds as your proper accoutrements. But if you are a lay follower (*upāsaka*), may your conduct be free from pride, and may you possess the proper accoutrements for your practice, such as a nose-towel.

Do not apply your mind to the essence of the sciences of logic (*tarka*), grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), the *āgamas*, *purāṇas*, and so forth, nor to the true doctrine (*saddharma*) of the *samaya-kośa*, the *kriyā-tantras*, and the like—especially since you have not applied yourself to the subject at hand: speech, song, dance, and so on. The fault in applying yourself [to those] is that the afflictions (*kleśa*) will increase; you will fail to eliminate the subject at hand: passion (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and delusion (*moha*), as well as death itself. If all of these are pursued, it is like a person who climbs a tree, reaches the top, and then falls down, suffering from illness and distress, always remaining far from liberation (*mokṣa*). However, we do not reject them entirely, for you may know them to yield results at all times, and to yield auspicious results through the attainment of liberation.

Furthermore, one should seek out a place such as a mountain peak, a forest, a seashore, or a location where there is a hut, a monastery (*vihāra*), a Dharma hall, or a hermitage (*alas*)—all of which are auspicious. It should be a place of divine power (*pahoman*), conducive to meditative absorption (*asamādhi*), suitable for ascetic practice (*paṣandyan*), ritual worship (*paṅarccanan*), and solitary retreat (*gṛhaśūnya*). This is the place for practicing the sacred observances (*samaya*), for lying down, for spreading out [a mat], and for consuming wine, meat, and whatever else one may eat.

Thus, even if there is suffering in the body during the night, it is not a fault for you to consume food; rather, it serves as a cause for the body to become complete, to produce happiness, to produce right knowledge (*samyajñāna*), and to produce meditative absorption (*samādhi*), which are the means for attaining the state of the liberated ones. Therefore, we say: do not eat unwholesome things, do not choose foods that are harmful, and furthermore, do not relish the taste of what you eat. That is the way to eat.
If you are a *marūpa* (ascetic), you must be adorned with bark garments, wearing a *maṇḍala* of ash, and carrying a water-strainer (*sopacāra*).

If you are a *buddharṣi*, you must likewise be adorned, smeared with ash and sandalwood paste, and carry a water-strainer as an article of ritual service. If you are a lay follower (*upāsaka*), you must perform your conduct according to the rules of the water-strainer, keeping the tip of your nose straight.

Do not concern yourself with the essence of the sciences of logic (*tarka*), grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), the Tantras, and so forth, nor with songs or discourses; what use is it for you to labor over such things? For *prakṛti*—namely passion (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and delusion (*moha*)—is like a tree that has grown tall, yet when it begins to decay and fall, it becomes withered and bears no fruit.

Thus, this is my command for you; you must heed it and comply. Do not fail to comply with us, nor do we exercise compulsion over your compliance with us; rather, it is because of the gravity of your failure to comply with us. Do not act thus. Listen well to our instruction: grasp the vision (*darśana*), the discernment (*pariccheda*), and the practice (*pratipatti*), which are its root, middle, and end; these shall quickly become infinite through constant practice. Do not be wavering, do not be negligent, lest you cause confusion regarding our teaching, just like Suvarṇapaṇḍita.

Regarding the *Siṅgih*, the *Vyākaraṇa*, the *Tantra*, and so forth—this is the name by which I am worthy to be called; it is that which I employ as my own, being the lineage of the grace (*varānugraha*) of the venerable Śrī Mahāmpuṅku, namely the divine essence of myself toward the feet of the venerable Śrī Mahāmpuṅku.

Oṃ! O sons of the Conqueror, we shall now explain to you the teachings that are worthy for you to practice. There is that which is called the *ṣaṭpāramitā* (the six perfections); these constitute the path to supreme enlightenment (*paramabodhimārgga*). We shall teach them to you, so that you may not find it difficult to practice for the sake of attaining the state of the Buddhas.
Herein are the details of those six perfections:
[b27] Generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditation, and wisdom.

The six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) are said to have the threefold characteristic of giving (*dāna*). They are: the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), the perfection of ethical conduct (*śīlapāramitā*), the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*), the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*), the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*), and the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). These are the types of perfections that serve as the means for attaining great awakening (*mahābodhi*). Regarding the "threefold characteristic of giving": there are three modes of the characteristic of giving, namely: giving (*dāna*), excessive giving (*atidāna*), and great excessive giving (*mahātidāna*).
As for the meaning of *dāna*:

"Furthermore, having given food and drink, gold and other jewels, wealth, clothing, beds and seats, royal glory, one's own property, and even one's city— if one gives these, they say that this is *dāna*."

Ka: What is the essence of giving? It is as follows: when one possesses wealth, such as a house, a wife, children, servants, or various things—whether they be gold, jewels, pearls, slaves, livestock, elephants, or horses—if someone comes to you to ask for them, do not fail to provide a reciprocal gift. Even if your heart is weary of that very state of being, you should still be generous toward those people who come to you; speak kind words, act with propriety, and be welcoming. This is what is called *dāna* (giving).

Having given even their own wives and beloved sons to others, they felt no further thirst for desire nor a trace of sorrow in their hearts; they say that such is the supreme gift, like that of the Lord of the Twice-born.

[28] Child, your wife, and likewise any woman who has requested this from you—just as the Great Being (Mahāsattva) meritoriously offered his wife, his son, and even the Brahmin who was his servant—the reason for this is that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the obstacle to attaining Buddhahood; it prevents one from reaching Buddhahood. Therefore, let your craving for her be severed. "Do not have even an atom’s worth of a sorrowful mind" (*hayva ta nāśokacittaṃ paramāṇumātra*). Such merit is the means for entering the City of Enlightenment (*bodhinagara*). This is the sequence of performing such merit, which is called *atikṛtadāna* (the gift of what has been fully prepared).
The meaning of "great supreme gift" (mahātidadana) is as follows:
"Having conquered the lord of the Asuras, he gave his own flesh and blood to others;
because of the power of his inheritance, he gave his heart and body, which were composed of the ninefold suffering—this the virtuous call the great supreme gift."

What are the limbs of that Great Being? His body, his blood, his eyes, and his own person—there is no craving for him in any of these. He has compassion for all beings, motivated by the suffering of those beings. Whether it be a *rākṣasa*, a beast, or a *garuḍa*, they are sacrificed by him for his body, his blood, and his eyes; he sacrifices them to aged Brahmins to test their heroic generosity, and his heart is sacrificed to the compassionate who grieve for the suffering of others. He causes his own body to perform good deeds for the sake of common folk, yet he feels no attachment to them. Such is the practice of merit; this is what is called the "Great Gift" (*mahā-dāna*).
Thus, indeed, is the description of the giving (*dāna*); its threefold division has been explained.
As for the perfection of ethical conduct (*śīlapāramitā*):
"Complete withdrawal from all that is unwholesome, and likewise engagement in what is wholesome."
Thus is the summary of ethical discipline (*śīla*) according to the sequence of body, speech, and mind. What is this? Body, speech, and mind.
"Body" (*kāya*) refers to the physical frame; the sixteen parts consisting of hands and feet—that is what is called "body."

Speech (*vāk*) means sound; all utterances are called speech. Mind (*citta*) means feeling; that is what is meant by mind. In brief: one should not perform evil with body, speech, or mind; in whatever way it is termed an evil deed, one must not engage in it. That which is called the "three bodies" (*trikāya*) consists of: body, speech, and mind.

What are the things that one should strive to perform with the three bodies? Good deeds—namely, all that is called *śubhakarma* (wholesome action)—these should be performed by means of the three bodies.
What are the types of *aśubhakarma* (unwholesome action) that one should not strive to perform with the body?
They are: abstaining from taking life (*prāṇātipātavirati*), abstaining from taking what is not given (*adattādānavirati*), and abstaining from sexual misconduct (*kāmamithyācāravirati*).

*Prāṇātipātavirati* means: not killing any living being (*prāṇī*) that is known, whether they are revered or lowly, with faults or without faults—indeed, as long as it is a living being—one does not cause it to be killed. What is the fault in killing them? It is because one will be driven into hell; for he who kills is the cause of hell, receiving an extreme burden of suffering, and taking birth as a *preta*, an animal, or even as insects, ants, and the like.

Abstaining from taking what is not given (*adattādānavirati*) means: not to take wealth that has not been bestowed; whether the wealth is valuable or worthless, one must not take it if the person does not wish to give it, even if both parties are in agreement. This is a cause for rebirth in hell, and furthermore, it constitutes a lack of faith toward the Lord, for His characteristics are not perceived within him.

*Kāmamithyācāravirati* means: not to engage in non-restraint with women. All types of women are considered unfit for possession (*parigraha*), namely: those with matted hair (*jaṭī*), those with topknots (*śikhī*), those with shaven heads (*muṇḍī*), those with necklaces of thorns (*sakaṇṭaka*), as well as the wives of one’s gurus and the female descendants of one’s own family. Even if a woman is beautiful, if she is in a temple (*devagṛha*) containing a Buddha image, a divine statue (*arccā*), a *pratimā*, a reliquary (*peṭa*), a scripture (*pustaka*), or in the dwelling place of one’s guru, one must not have sexual intercourse with her. What is the fault in doing so? It is a cause for hell, and furthermore, it causes the fruit of your yoga, vows, and meditative absorption (*samādhi*) to vanish because of her.

[31] Regarding the *wirati* (vow) of the *saṅkerikā*: how many are there that are suitable to be undertaken by the body? It is one who does not become restless in foot or restless in hand, and whose head is not touched by others while receiving the *sambhāra* offerings. As for the faults that would touch it: the Lord, the five *Tathāgatas*, are on his head; this is why the *saṃskāras* are said to adorn his head with the *sambhāra* offerings, for the lotus of the Lord Buddha is dissolved when his head is adorned by the village. Furthermore, he does not enter the house of a *caṇḍāla*, because the true nature (*tattva*) of his body is the abode of the Buddhas once the Buddha-consecration (*buddhābhiṣeka*) has been performed. The Lord Buddha is the Supreme Lord of Supreme Lords, the *Sarvadevatāguru*, the teacher of all deities. This is the reason why it is not permitted to perform acts of degradation (*adhaḥkriyā*) toward him, nor to treat him with disrespect (*upadhāna*). This is the reason why one does not consort with women, considering them as the wives of one’s teacher (*gurupatnī*), and why no person may consort with him, for he is the cause of his own self-origination (*svotpādakahetu*), the very essence of the Lord Sugata. He becomes the causal agent himself, and his teaching is maintained by the followers of the Sugata. Therefore, the state of not consorting with women, whose heads have not been adorned by the consecrated *sambhāra* offerings, and who does not engage in acts of degradation—that is what is suitable to be undertaken by such a person.
Why do you not wish to act according to her?

The sequence of these [precepts] is as follows: abstain from false speech; abstain from slander; abstain from harsh speech; abstain from idle chatter; abstain from eating all kinds of food, beginning with onions; do not find fault with the virtues or lack of virtues in others; and do not engage in sexual intercourse with women. Do not eat near a *acyuta* (a tree sacred to the Buddha); do not engage in sexual intercourse with women; do not eat near an *acyuta*; do not eat near a *vedānta-nivedya* (food offered to the Vedānta deities) or to Lord Buddha. Such is the path that should be well practiced by those who are called "wise" (*vāk*).
Why is it that the mind does not produce what is good?

He is free from attachment (*rāga*), free from aversion (*dveṣa*), free from delusion (*moha*), free from hypocrisy (*dambha*), free from envy (*īrṣyā*), and free from stinginess (*mātsaryya*); furthermore, he is free from anger (*krodha*), free from gain (*lābha*), and free from sorrow (*śoka*). Moreover, he possesses purity (*śuci*) and truthfulness (*satya*), and avoids falsehood (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). He regards all sentient beings with reverence, possesses deep spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), and maintains devotion toward the Lord Pañcatathāgata as well as toward the Lord Ratnatraya. (He is one who) is able to liberate all sentient beings from the suffering of *saṃsāra*; this is what is called being "well-practiced" by means of the mind.
In brief: the attainment of complete purity of body, speech, and mind is called the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).
The perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*) is defined as:
"A mind that is equal toward friend and foe, and equal toward those who offer honor and those who do not."
One should call the practice of peace and gentleness toward those who are angry the perfection of patience.

What is this mind that is weary of the many kinds of suffering? It is that which dwells within you, yet lacks consistency in body, lacks consistency in speech, and lacks consistency in mind; it is not ill, nor is it joyful, as if one were about to fall into misfortune. It is merely the consequence of past karmic transgressions, without the capacity to reflect upon all sentient beings. Furthermore, you have been instructed and exhorted by me; do not be agitated, do not be elated, do not be distressed or dejected, and maintain equanimity toward all sentient beings.
In brief: there is no transformation of the mind regarding that which is being contemplated and investigated. That state is what is called the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*).
As for the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*): it is the exertion of vigor day and night for the sake of bringing about the welfare of sentient beings.
It does not produce anything that is outflowing; this is remembered as the perfection of vigor.

What is that body which acts with the mind? It is as follows: when one is not heedless, then one does not fail to perform wholesome deeds (*kuśalakarmma*) by day and by night. The types of wholesome deeds to be performed by day are: transcribing the True Dharma (*saddharma*), making offerings, giving clarified butter (*ājya*), writing the sacred syllables (*ākāra pallawa*), mental cultivation (*manasi*), reciting the True Dharma, offering the sacred Dharma to books, providing materials for stupas (*sthūpopakāraṇa*), beginning the construction of a stupa or an image of the Tathāgata, performing worship with all necessary requisites, performing fire sacrifices (*homa*), and practicing meditation and contemplation in solitude. Such are the types of wholesome deeds to be performed by that body, speech, and mind during the day.
What wholesome deeds should one perform with body, speech, and mind during the night?

Recitation, application, meditation, and the chanting of mantras in praise of the Honored Ones of all the Tathāgatas and all the Goddesses—by means of these, one benefits all sentient beings and brings about their well-being; they transcend the realm of rebirth, break free from the wheel of existence (*bhāvacakra*), attain a happy destiny, and enter into supramundane bliss (*lokottarasukha*). Such is the practice of virtue performed by body, speech, and mind, without distinction and without deficiency, which does not encounter difficulty. That state is what is called the Perfection of Vigor (*vīryapāramitā*).
The perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā) is defined as follows:
"The yogin’s mind of constant compassion toward the superior, middling, and inferior truths, arising from the power of yoga, is known as the perfection of meditation."

Kaḥ: Kaṅ Āmběk (the Embryo) is that which remains in solitude (*ekānta*) within all beings (*sarvasattva*), whether they be inferior, middling, or superior (*kaniṣṭha-madhyama-uttama*). He constantly contemplates their welfare and peace both here and hereafter, even beyond this entire world. How does He contemplate their welfare and peace among all beings? By making Himself one with them. What is the nature of this Embryo? "He who is *satva* (being), that indeed am I; he who is I, that is all *satva*. This is the primordial form (*ākāra*). The body of all beings is my body, and my body is the body of all beings; for all things (*avibhāga-eka-svabhāva*) are without distinction from all phenomena (*sarvadharma*). Such is the reason for the Embryo. This is what is called the Perfection of Meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*).
The Perfection of Wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is defined as follows:
"As many things as there are, situated in the ten directions, they are all empty by nature; this is remembered as the Perfection of Wisdom."

What is meant by "many" (*bahutva*) established in the ten directions (*daśadiksaṃsthita*) in this world? It refers to those that exist in the ten regions: east, south, west, north, southeast, southwest, northwest, northeast, above, and below. This is understood as extending to the body, both external and internal, as well as all sentient beings, all sciences (*vidyā*), all actions (*kriyā*), all castes (*varṇa*), and all factions (*pakṣa*). This is understood through its having form (*sākāra*) and its being formless (*nirākāra*), which is the nature of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). The connection is this: there is no perception when one perceives the nature of unity and multiplicity (*ekāneka-svabhāva*), because the singular and the many meet and converge—that which is called "many. When one perceives it, there is no meeting with the essence (*tattva*) of the object of cognition (*grāhya*); when one perceives it, there is no meeting with that which is called the absolute singular (*tuhutuhu tunggal*). When the perception continues, one perceives that which is devoid of the absolute singular called "many. Even regarding external objects (*bāhyavastu*), such a reality (*tattva*) is not met with in sequence; thus it reaches the nature of consciousness (*jñānasvarūpa*), where there is no perception of that which is both singular and multiple in the form of the grasped (*grāhya*). Furthermore, if the form of the grasper (*grāhakākāra*) is non-grasping (*agrāhaka*), and the non-grasped (*agrāhya*) is its reality (*tattva*), then its duality is not met; indeed, its duality is pleasant within the emptiness of the single nature (*ekasvabhāva*). Emptiness is the single nature of all phenomena (*sarvadharmma*). Furthermore, whether external or internal, the momentary perception is what is called emptiness; the reality of the form of the grasped or the form of the grasper is not met at all, and the activity (*pravṛtti*) of that consciousness (*jñāna*) remains constant. One should practice that emptiness like a meditative state (*bhāvanā*) where the body itself is not met.

This discourse has concluded regarding the nature of the grasped and the grasper. Finally, that which is devoid of all phenomena (*sarvaprapañcavarjita*)—the wisdom that transcends all phenomena and is free from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) within existence and non-existence—is the attainment of a state beyond activity. Its essence is like space (*ākāśamata*), vast, unobstructed, and as ancient as space itself. Therefore, this reality is called *prajñāpāramitā*, which is practiced by the venerable ones who possess all supernatural powers (*sarvasiddhi*); for this reason, it leads to the state of Buddhahood.
Thus, this is not the characteristic of having attained what is called the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).
O sons of the Conquerors belonging to the lineage of the Tathāgatas who are engaged in higher practice, you must cultivate the four perfections.
The four perfections are: loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).

The meaning of *maitrī* is: *parahitākṛtva*, the form of the knowledge of one who is distinguished among beings (*sattvaviśeṣa*). One who is distinguished among beings is defined as one who practices the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) and the four perfections (*catuḥpāramitā*); he is called *sattvaviśeṣa*. The nature of his knowledge is to create welfare for others. "Others" means all sentient beings—whether inferior, middling, or superior. That love toward others which is not contingent upon a reward is what is called *maitrī*.

Compassion (*karuṇā*) means: "And [the desire] for the separation from the suffering of others. It is the aspect of the knowledge of a superior being (*satvaviśeṣa*) that aims to eliminate the suffering of all superior beings; compassion is defined as follows: the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkatā*), the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāraduḥkatā*), and the suffering of change (*pariṇāmaduḥkatā*). These are the three types of suffering. The suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkatā*) means: the experience of pain resulting from one's own birth and its consequences, such as in the case of human birth. As for the mother, she gives birth to him, and he then undergoes the suffering of labor and so forth; this is what is called the suffering of suffering.

The nature of suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) is as follows: the cycle of evil rebirths [is such that] one encounters a womb; just as when a person is born, they die, and then that same person is born again. This is what is called the nature of suffering inherent in conditioned formations.

The suffering of transformation (*pariṇāmaduḥkatā*) means: its characteristic is that after one has finished experiencing a birth, one subsequently undergoes another birth greater than that previous birth in its consequences; for example, as in the case of a human birth, when one dies due to lack of heedfulness regarding the Dharma, one is born again as a deity, yet due to that very heedlessness, one is born again as a human. This is what is called the suffering of transformation.
This is not the threefold suffering. The way in which a sentient being experiences such suffering is due to the compassion (*karuṇā*) of a superior being (*satva viśeṣa*).

There are three types of compassion to be known: compassion directed toward sentient beings (*sattvālambanakaruṇā*), compassion directed toward phenomena (*dharmālambanakaruṇā*), and objectless compassion (*anālambanakaruṇā*). This is the threefold classification of compassion.

Compassion having sentient beings as its object (*satvālambanakaruṇā*) means: "The compassion of those who have not abandoned the view of self, which has suffering sentient beings as its object. The nature of this compassion is such that one performs compassion toward those sentient beings who are currently experiencing suffering; having performed loving-kindness (*maitrī*), this is the compassion of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). Such is the compassion of worldlings, which is called "compassion having sentient beings as its object."

Compassion having phenomena as its object (*dharmālambanakaruṇā*) means: "Compassion directed toward conditioned things (*saṃskāra*) for those who have abandoned the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), which is suffering. This compassion is practiced by one who possesses no grasping; it is the act of bringing relief from suffering to sentient beings. Having as its basis the suffering of sentient beings, it is the practice of compassion. After having practiced loving-kindness (*maitrī*), this is the "compassion of the Noble One, the Great Being, having phenomena as its object" (*mahāsatvasya āryasya dharmālambanā karuṇā*). Just as is the compassion of the Noble One, the Great Being, that is called *dharmālambanakaruṇā*.

Non-referential compassion (*anālambana-karuṇā*) is as follows: for those who have abandoned the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and are established upon the Path, there is compassion that proceeds without an object of reference. Compassion is the state of having no attachment toward sentient beings; it is called compassion because one acts without attachment toward phenomena (*dharma*). Having already cultivated loving-kindness (*maitrī*), one performs compassion toward sentient beings who are suffering. For Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who are free from attachment to the grasped and the grasper (*grāhya-grāhakābhiniveśavigata*), there is non-referential compassion. Just as the compassion of a Bodhisattva is without grasping, so too is the compassion of a Bodhisattva without an object of reference; this is what is called "non-referential compassion."

Thus, compassion (*karuṇā*) is not differentiated here. Merely through the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*)—without wavering in wisdom, like the mind of a child within its mother’s womb—that is called the *Jambhala-samādhi*.
The state of non-dual yoga (*advayayoga*) that knows the reality (*tattva*) like the intellect of a *manuk wāhu* bird that has entered its nest is called the *vāgīśvarasamādhi*.

The state of non-duality together with wisdom (*prajñā*) and compassion (*karuṇā*) toward all sentient beings is called the *lokeśvarasamādhi*. The state of non-duality together with the vajra-anger and compassion toward all sentient beings is called the *vajrasatvasamādhi*.

The practice of non-duality (*advaya*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) that possesses a heart of affection for all sentient beings is called the *muniwaracintāmaṇi-samādhi*. The practice of non-duality and wisdom that serves as a dwelling place for the repeated instruction regarding what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted for all sentient beings is called the *śvetaketu-samādhi*.

The sound of the wind is the sound of the *karĕgĕp* (the internal fire); the body is shaken by the wind, and the body takes on the form of the sun. When the body vanishes, it is dissolved by the wind, which has the sound of *aḥ*. There is liberation (*mukṣa*) without fainting; there is no inhalation or exhalation of the wind, and the movement of the wind ceases. The body and the mind cease to exist. Just as a flame becomes extinguished, he makes the night his dwelling, free from obscuration (*nirāvaraṇa*), formless (*nirākāra*), day and night, at all times. This is called the *Kumāranirbbāṇa-cittamai-samādhi*.

[b47] The *kapiṅpitu* is the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that is the foundation for cultivating the mind in the state of liberation, so as to attain final emancipation (*mokṣa*). Furthermore, this is our instruction to you:
the body is within the interior of the *stūpa* and the temple (*prāsāda*). As for its meaning in terms of the syllables: *NAMAḤ SIDDHAṂ A, Ā; I, Ī; U, Ū; RĔ, RÖ; LĔ, LÖ; E, AI; O, AU, AṄ, AḤ*.
