All thirty-seven syllables are of the nature of non-duality; they are *aroka* (light) and *kleśa* (affliction), which are mutually intermingled. This is the body of the *stūpa* within the temple (*prāsāda*); indeed, the *stūpa* and the temple are the body, for that is the abode of the Lord Buddha in his form of perfect tranquility (*samāhita-rūpa*). O sons of the Conqueror (*jinaputra*), you who have been instructed by me, you should understand this according to the Mahāyāna teachings.

I shall now give you another instruction concerning me and you: let not others see your body or hear your voice; let your tongue be radiant like the sun, your eyes radiant like the sun, your nostrils radiant like the sun, your ears radiant like the sun, your heart, your very core, your neck, your shoulders, your elbows, your wrists, your palms, and your feet—all radiant like the sun. Even your entire body, from within out, is thus; in this way, your body will become beautiful. This is called "radiance like the sun": it is the state of being free from all afflictions throughout your entire body, so that your body, my dear, becomes luminous.

The breath flows upward and downward, reaching as far as the high blue [heavens]. One should restrain it within the hollow of the *huntuta* (the cranial vault), where the upper and lower breaths meet. One should draw the wind through the mouth and force it into the navel; one should suppress that wind so that it is steady and not agitated. That subtle wind, which cannot be obstructed, is drawn up and suppressed. Likewise, when the blood-borne wind becomes the *aṃ*, it emits the sun, complete and full of power, which enters your body. When that has occurred, the mind becomes radiant, pure, and free from obscuration, like the time of the midday sun. Such a state of absorption is called *kahyaṅbuddhān*; its name is Maṇik Sarwasaparipūraka. Practice this again and again, for such is the way to attain *kahyaṅbuddhān*.

Furthermore, there is that which is called the sevenfold samādhi, namely: when one restrains the breath (*bāyu*) of inhalation and exhalation, and remains still within the abdomen without wavering, such that there is no longer any perception of its presence or absence—that is called *jambhalasamādhi*; this is *pūrvvasamādhi*. Once the breath has been mastered and restrained, the body must not be made rigid; rather, the abdomen becomes supple like the mind of a well-trained bird when it settles upon its perch. Being aware of the purity of body, speech, and mind, one becomes supple and stainless. Such an abdomen is called *vāgīśwarasamādhi*.

When one has seen all sentient beings as being stained by passion and the other afflictions, one becomes the "Ambek" (the Crushing One) who subdues the hearts of all sentient beings; even though they have not yet repaid one’s kindness, such an Ambek is called the *lokeśvarasamādhi*. When one becomes the Ambek who wields the fierce *vajra* to crush the minds of all the wicked and subdue the hearts of everyone, such an Ambek is called the *vajrasatvasamādhi*.

Furthermore, that *āmběk* is the *Ādibuddha* of the Universal Monarch (*cakravartti-rāja*) who has already subdued his enemies; his power is vast and capable of fulfilling the desires of all sentient beings (*sarvasattva*). Such an *āmběk* is called the *Mahāmuniwara-cintāmaṇi-samādhi*. Furthermore, that *āmběk* is the vigor (*utsāha*) of all sentient beings toward their practice of the Dharma. Such an *āmběk* is called the *Śvetaketu-samādhi*.

That mind, which is radiant like the face of Nirvāṇa, is as bright as the full sun; it is radiant throughout the day, unobscured, and never ceases for even a moment—this is called the Samādhi of the Youthful Nirvāṇa.

Now, furthermore, one must strive to discern those who are intent upon attaining liberation. The wind on the right is named Amitābha; the wind on the left is named Amoghasiddhi; the wind that emerges from the rear is named Ratnasambhava; the wind that does not emerge from either the left or the right is named Akṣobhya; and the wind at the end [of the cycle] is named Vairocana. Their location is at the top of the nostrils, inwardly in the *uṣṇīṣa*. These five are the stainless, pure purities; they are indeed known as the Five Noble Tastes (*pañcarasa*).

Furthermore, when the wind of the right-hand *karmmaprasara* arises, it produces the fire-maṇḍala, which is triangular in shape, filled with a red color, and has a trident (*triśūla*) in its center; this is the means for accomplishing all rites (*sarvakarma*). Alternatively, one may produce the Mahendra-maṇḍala from the wind of the right-hand *apasarga*; it is filled with a golden color, and has a five-pronged vajra (*pañcaśūcikavajra*) upon it; this is the means for accomplishing the increase of life and the increase of wealth.
Furthermore, one should place the Mahendramaṇḍalāpasarga; its color is white and its essence is lunar (somya); it is the vajra in the center for the sake of attaining stability in that very state.

The four mandalas of the *agramaṇḍala* serve for subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*) and attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*). In the left exhalation, one generates the formless wind mandala; its color is black, blue, green, or yellow. It has two prongs, and its emblem is a banner and flag, while the left hand holds a hook and an earring. Its application is for the rite of attraction; however, for the rite of paralyzing (*sthāmbana*), one should utter [the mantra] and furthermore generate that water mandala in the left exhalation. It is long, its color is white, and in its center is a subtle, beautiful mandala, like pure crystal; this serves as its central color and emblem. Its application is for the rite of pacification (*śāntika*).

As for that supreme, extraordinary wind (*paramaviśeṣavāyu*), it does not move as the breath (*uśwāsa*); it is solely radiant, free from obstruction, formless, and it enters the region of the nose, reaching into the interior up to the *uṣṇīṣa*. It is pure, clean, and cannot be grasped; this is called the *Vairocana-samādhi*. One should strive to conceal it, so that it cannot be seen by others. When one is angry with another, it serves to destroy evil; when one is pleased, it serves to make people devoted and to cause them to honor the lineage of the Guru.

Thus ends the Great Instruction on the Supreme Samaya of the Noble Mahāyāna, concerning that which is to be awakened: the mind should not be confused; this is the conclusion of his symbolic teaching, the essence of wisdom.

Īṃ! O Great Sage, please listen to me, the venerable Śrī Mahāmpuṅku. The noble one who has taken form as the mouth of Lord Buddha is Śrī Mahāmpuṅku. As for the description of that other learned master: the Three Jewels (Ratnatraya) and the Five Tathāgatas are his mouths—Lord Buddha, Śuddha, Nīla, Pītta, Rakta, and Viśwavarṇa; their hand gestures (mudrās) are the banner (dhvaja), earth-touching (bhūḥsparśa), boon-granting (varada), meditative (dhyāna), and fear-dispelling (abhaya). Such is the description of that other learned master, which causes you, my son Mahāmpuṅku, to have doubt regarding knowledge. Therefore, let the venerable Śrī Mahāmpuṅku investigate this, so that this doubtful knowledge may vanish and right knowledge (samyajñāna) may arise.

Auṃ! We are of the Tathāgata family, O sons of the Jinas; listen well to this. There are three divisions of *jñāna*: external (*vāhyaka*), with form (*sākāra*), and formless (*nirākāra*). If the Lord is manifested as the very embodiment of the Lord Buddha, that is formless *jñāna*, which is His cause and is the grasper (*grāhaka*) of Him. The Lord Buddha is worshipped by means of that *jñāna* with form (*sākāra*), namely Śrī Mānakālenga, as follows: Just as the Lord Buddha is bodiless yet possesses the form of a deity, He arises from the syllable *kṛikāra* of white color, with the *dhvajamudrā*; He is the Lord named Śrī Śākyamuni. [a53] *SARVVADEVAGURŪCYATE*, meaning He is called the Guru of all deities. A deity emerges from the body of the Lord Śrī Śākyamuni to the right, red in color, with the *dhyānamudrā*, originating from the syllable *hriḥ*; He is the Lord named Śrī Lokeśwara. A deity emerges from the body of Śrī Śākyamuni to the left, blue in color, with the *bhūḥsparśamudrā*, originating from the syllable *brīḥ*; He is the Lord named Śrī Bajrapāṇi. These three Lords are known as the Three Jewels (*ratnatraya*); they are designated as Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha. They possess the essence of body, speech, and mind; they possess the virtue of love, merit, and devotion, and they pervade the three worlds (*tribhuwana*). The Lord Śrī Vairocana emerges from the face of Śrī Śākyamuni. The Lord Śrī Lokeśwara divides himself, and the Lords Amitābha and Ratnasambhava emerge. The Lord Śrī Bajrapāṇi divides himself, and the Lords Amitābha and Amoghasiddhi emerge. These five are designated as the Five Tathāgatas, and another name for them is the Lord Sarvajñāna. From the Lord Sarvajñāna Vairocana, the deity Sarvakāryyakartta emerges; his manifestations are Īśwara, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu. He is made to fulfill the three worlds and to encompass their contents through the power of Lord Vairocana, for the purpose of benefiting others (*parārthān*). This is the place where the Lord is worshipped at all times, becoming all things stationary and moving. He bestows heaven upon the gods and so forth, the mortal realm upon humans and so forth, and the underworld (*pātāla*) upon the *nāgas* and so forth, by the power of the Lords Īśwara, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu. That is why he is called Sarvakāryyakartta; there is nothing that does not exist within him, yet it is manifested by the power of the Lord Śrī Vairocana as the Lord Sarvakāryyakartta, Īśwara, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu. Such is the manifestation of the Lord Sarvajña through the *jñāna* with form (*sākāra-jñāna*); He is worshipped through the *jñānatatva* with the six offerings (*ṣaḍupacāra*). Furthermore, He is manifested through the external *jñāna* (*vāhyaka-jñāna*) as the venerable image, the statue, and the vessel.

Śākali, perform the sixfold external service (ṣaḍupacāra) for a long time. Regarding the lineage of Kaliṅga: the Lord manifested himself as the Lord Ratnatraya; from him descended the Lord Pañcatathāgata. Pañcatathāgata gave birth to Pañceśvara; Pañceśvara gave birth to Brahmarṣi; and Brahmarṣi gave birth to all living beings, gods, and so forth. Understand this with certainty; have no doubt!

[54] Now, O Tattvaviśeṣa, listen further to my words concerning you regarding the sequence of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) for the Lord of Yogins: form (*rūpa*), sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Form is to be known as Vairocana; sensation is Ratnasambhava;
perception is Amitābha; and mental formations are the source of Amoghasiddhi.
Akṣobhya is consciousness (*vijñāna*); he is known as the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), the five limbs, and the five awakenings, whose nature consists of the five Tathāgatas.
Ka and ḍaṅ are Vairocana, who is form (*rūpa*). Form means: skin, flesh, bone, marrow, blood, lymph, and spinal fluid; that is what is called form.

The noble Lord Ratnasambhava is sensation (*vedanā*). Sensation means that which experiences pleasure and pain; that is sensation. The noble Lord Amitābha is perception (*saṃjñā*). Perception means name; "name" means designation; that is perception. The noble Lord Amoghasiddhi is mental formations (*saṃskāra*). Mental formations means that which acts as causes and conditions; that is mental formations.

Furthermore, the venerable Akṣobhya is *vijñāna*. *Vijñāna* means *samyagjñāna* (right knowledge). *Samyagjñāna* means direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*); that is what is called *vijñāna*.

The term *skandha* refers to the body, and the term *pañca* refers to the five; thus, it is called the "fivefold body. Such is the nature of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) for the Lord of Yogins (*yogīśvara*). Herein is the sequence of the seed-syllables (*bījākṣara*) that produce the five Tathāgatas: *aḥ*, *hūṃ*, *traṃ*, *hrīḥ*, *aḥ*.
Vairocana is the seed-syllable *AḤ*; likewise, Akṣobhya is the seed-syllable *HŪṂ*, Ratnasaṃbhava is *TRAṂ*, and Amitābha is *HRĪḤ*.

*AḤ* is the seed-syllable of Amoghasiddhi. The seed-syllable *AḤ* is the essence-mantra (*bīja*) and the deity Vairocana; the seed-syllable *HŪṂ* is the essence-mantra and the deity Akṣobhya; the seed-syllable *TRAṂ* is the essence-mantra and the deity Ratnasaṃbhava; the seed-syllable *HRĪḤ* is the essence-mantra and the deity Amitābha; and *AḤ* is the seed-syllable and the deity Amoghasiddhi.
This is the method for purifying the seed-syllables of the five Buddhas.

Herein is the procedure for the Lord Buddha regarding the three impurities (*trikhala*). The three impurities are: passion (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and delusion (*moha*); within these are included hypocrisy (*dambha*), envy (*īrṣyā*), and stinginess (*mātsarya*).
"Amītabha is to be known as Passion, and Hatred is Akṣobhyavajradṛk."

And delusion (*moha*) is also Vairocana; thus they exist as three forms. That which is passion (*rāga*) is the essence (*tattva*) of the noble Amitābha; that which is hatred (*dveṣa*) is the essence of the noble Akṣobhya; that which is delusion is the essence of Vairocana. These are what are called the "three stains" (*trikhala*) of the Lord of Yogins (*yogīśvara*). The cause of the confusion regarding the three states of existence is these [three]: passion, hatred, and delusion. "The three states of existence" means the wheel of existence (*bhāvacakra*).
Herein is the essence of the three impurities (*trimala*) in the Lord of Yogins:
Meaning is Śākyamuni; Desire is said to be Lokeśvara; Sound is to be known as Vajrapāṇi; these three impurities are held by the masters of yoga to be the object of practice.

*Artha* is the manifestation of the reality of Śrī Śākyamuni; *kāma* is the manifestation of the reality of Śrī Lokeśvara; *śabda* is the manifestation of the reality of Śrī Vajrapāṇi. These meanings—artha, kāma, and śabda—are that which the masters of yoga purify of the three impurities (*trimala*).
The Buddha consists of passion, hatred, and delusion, and is composed of wealth, desire, and sound;
for the sake of the cultivation of the right mindfulness of Dharma, there shall be the endurance of suffering through mindfulness.

Lord Buddha, whose nature is free from passion (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and delusion (*moha*), has as his purpose the [attainment of] *artha*, *kāma*, and *śabda*. What are these three evils (*trikhala*) and three impurities (*trimala*)? Their meaning is this: they consist of the lack of mindfulness (*asmṛti*) regarding the essence of the Dharma (*dharmma-marma*), the absence of recollection (*smṛti*) toward the Dharma, and that which leads to the persistence of suffering (*duḥkha-kadhāraṇā*). These are the causes that produce the three evils and the three impurities; they are the cause of suffering. So that the entire world may desire to practice the Dharma, these means (*sādhana*) have been taught for the sake of understanding what is difficult to grasp.
The Buddha is Śākyamuni, the Dharma is Lokeśvara the Lord, and the Saṅgha is to be known as Vajrapāṇi; these three are established as the Triple Gem.

Ka: The noble Śrī Śākyamuni is the ultimate reality (paramārtha-tattva) and the noble Buddha-tattva; the noble Lokeśvara is the Dharma-tattva; and the noble Vajrapāṇi is the noble Saṅgha-tattva. These are collectively designated as the Lord Ratnatraya (the Triple Gem). Furthermore, Vairocana, Amitābha, and Akṣobhya are the Ratnatraya. Moreover, Vairocana, Ratnasambhava, and Amoghasiddhi are another set of the Ratnatraya. Herein lies the reality of the three bodies (trikāya): body, speech, and mind. *Kāyo Vairocanaś cāpi vāk cāmitābho vijñeyaḥ* (The Body is indeed Vairocana, and Speech is to be known as Amitābha.)

Mind is Akṣobhyavajra and is considered the name for the three bodies (*trikāya*). The body of Lord Vairocana consists of all mudrās and all characteristics; that is what is meant by "body. The speech of Lord Amitābha is "speech"; speech means all sounds, beginning with mantras and seed-syllables (*bīja-akṣara*); that is what is meant by "speech."

Indeed, the noble Akṣobhya is the mind; that which is called the mind is omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). This is the reason why the Lord Ratnatraya possesses the three bodies (*trikāya*), as stated by the Lord Yogīśvara.
Herein is the essence of the three supreme aims (*triparārtha*) to be understood; "the three supreme aims" means: love (*asih*), merit (*puṇya*), and devotion (*bhakti*).
*Asiḥ vairocano jñeyaḥ puṇyaś cāmitābhas tathā* Vairocana is to be known as *asiḥ* (the sword), and Amitābha likewise as *puṇya* (merit).
And devotion (*bhakti*) is the unshakeable Vajra-vision; it is said to have three supreme purposes.

*Ka:* Lord Vairocana is the sword. "Sword" means one who masters the four perfections (*caturpāramitā*); that is what is meant by the sword. Lord Amitābha is merit (*puṇya*). That which constantly practices the essence of the *āgama*, attains and maintains austerity (*tapa*), vows (*vrata*), consecration (*saṃskāra*), and the Buddha’s teaching, and never ceases to practice the Dharma—that is called devotion (*bhakti*).
The love of meritorious devotion is the ultimate goal consisting of the threefold purpose; it has the nature of the Three Jewels.
Herein is the nature of the five elements (*pañcadhātu*) for the Lord of Yogins (*yogīśvara*). The five elements are: earth, water, fire, wind, and space.
Pṛthivīdhātu is Buddha, and Abdhātu is Ratnasambhava.
The fire element is Amitābha, the wind element is Amoghasiddhi,
and the space element is Akṣobhya; these five elements, along with the sentient being and the five bodies, have the nature of the five Tathāgatas.
Lord Vairocana is the Buddha; he is the earth element (*pṛthivīdhātu*). That which has the nature of hardness is called earth.

Lord Ratnasambhava is the water element (*āpaḥdhātu*). That which has the nature of fluidity is called water. Lord Amitābha is the fire element (*tejadhātu*). That which has the nature of lightness is called the fire element.

The noble Lord Amoghasiddhi is the wind element (*vāyudhātu*). That which has the nature of movement is what is called the wind element. The noble Lord Akṣobhya is the space element (*ākāśadhātu*). That which has the nature of emptiness is what is called space.
Such is the sequence of the five Tathāgatas who produce the five elements.

The five elements (*pañcadhātu*) are that which constitutes the body of all sentient beings (*sarvasattva*), namely: earth as the foundation, skin, flesh, and bone; water as the fluids, lymph, marrow, semen, and phlegm; fire as the digestive heat; wind as the breath; and space as the cavities of the body and the hair. Such is the enumeration of the five great elements (*pañcamahābhūta*) that constitute the physical basis of all sentient beings, together with their respective qualities (*guṇa*), which form the body: earth has the quality of smell (*gandha*); water has the quality of taste (*rasa*); fire has the quality of form (*rūpa*); wind has the quality of touch (*sparśa*); and space has the quality of sound (*śabda*). This is the reason why the *puruṣa* is perceived through form, taste, smell, touch, and sound, for it possesses these five elements as its constituent basis.

Now follows the sequence of the venerable Tathāgatas who originate from the five aggregates of form (*pañca-rūpaskandha*). The five aggregates of form are: *kalala*, *arvuda*, *ghana*, *peśī*, and *praśāka*.
*Kalala* is Vajrasattva, and *Arvuda* is Ratnasambhava; *Ghana* is to be known as Amitābha, and *Peśī* is Amoghasiddhi.
Vairocana is the body of peace, arising from the nature of the five forms;
through the perfect awakening of the five aspects, he is considered the five Tathāgatas.
The noble Lord Akṣobhya is the *kalala*. *Kalala* means the morbid mass (*pilapilu*). The noble Lord Ratnasambhava is the *arvuda*. *Arvuda* means the bubble (*wĕrĕh*).

The venerable Lord Amitābha is *ghana*. *Ghana* means a solid mass, such as a clod of earth, like a cow, a horse, and so forth. The venerable Lord Amoghasiddhi is *peśi*. *Peśi* means a soft mass, such as an ant, and so forth. The venerable Lord Vairocana is *praśaka*. *Praśaka* means a head, a torso, or a limb, such as a human being, a deity, and so forth.
This is the sequence of the five Tathāgatas, who are the five aggregates (*skandha*), whose nature is the fivefold perfect awakening.
This is the sequence of the knowledge of the five Tathāgatas according to the noble Mahāyāna:
the Buddha of Eternal Knowledge and Akṣobhya of Mirror-like Knowledge.
Samatā is Ratnasambhava; Kṛtyānuṣṭhāna is Amoghasiddhi; Pratyavekṣaṇā is to be known as Lokeśvara, the supreme bliss.
These five gnoses are proclaimed as the secret.

[b59] What is non-conceptual knowledge (*niṣprapañca-jñāna*)? It is that which is characterized by the absence of clinging to a self; this is called "eternal knowledge" (*śāśvata-jñāna*), and it is the knowledge of Lord Vairocana. That which is radiant knowledge (*prabhāsvara-jñāna*), shining like the splendor of the divine sun, is called "knowledge of non-perception" (*adarśana-jñāna*); this is the knowledge of Lord Akṣobhya. That knowledge which is devoid of the grasped and the grasper, which does not cling, and whose body does not cling, is called "space-like knowledge" (*ākāśamata-jñāna*); this is the knowledge of Lord Ratnasambhava.

The wisdom of the selflessness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmanairātmyajñāna*), which constantly realizes the emptiness of all phenomena, is called the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇajñāna*); this is the wisdom of Lord Amitābha. The wisdom that functions in all activities and exists everywhere, subsequently manifesting as the conduct of the self, is called the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*); this is the wisdom of Lord Amoghasiddhi.
For this reason, Lord Amoghasiddhi is called *Karmakūli*, because of his activity in all actions.
This is the classification of the five *tathāgata*-wisdoms (*pañcajñāna*) by that Lord of Yogins; it is a supreme secret. Herein is the sequence of the five *tathāgata*-consorts (*devī*);
their enumeration is as follows: Bharālī Dhātvīśvarī, Bharālī Māmakī, Bharālī Pāṇḍaravāsinī, and Bharālī Tārā. Thus, each of them is fivefold.
Dhātvīśvarī, the Great Goddess, is to be known as the consort of Vairocana.
Locanā is the consort of Akṣobhya, and Dhātvīśvarī is the consort of Vairocana;
Māmakī is the consort of Ratnasambhava, and the goddess Pāṇḍaravāsinī is to be known as the consort of Amitābha; Tārā is the beloved of Amoghasiddhi.

*Bharālī* Dhātvīśvarī is the goddess on the head; she is the Mistress (*makaswāmi*) of Lord Vairocana. *Bharālī* Locanā is the Mistress of Lord Akṣobhya. *Bharālī* Dhātvīśvarī and *Bharālī* Locanā are of one and the same essence (*tatwa*); this refers to those four goddesses who are the great assistants (*sumahakārya*) of Lord Vairocana, whose abode is the eternal abode (*śāśwatajñāna*), the abode of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*), and the form of omniscience (*sarvajñarūpa*). Their varieties are: Satvavajrī, Ratnavajrī, Dharmavajrī, and Karmavajrī. Such are the varieties of the four goddesses who are the retinue (*parivāra*) of Lord Vairocana. As for how they may be worshipped by the practitioner (*saṅ sādhaka*), it is so that he may attain the state of Vairocana. *Bharālī* Māmakī is the goddess of Lord Ratnasambhava. *Bharālī* Pāṇḍaravāsinī is the goddess of Lord Amitābha. *Bharālī* Tārā is the goddess of Lord Amoghasiddhi. Such is the sequence of the six Tathāgatas together with their goddesses.
[61] These seed-syllables are assigned to the four goddesses: E, Vaṃ, Ma, and Ya.
The syllable E is known as Māmakī; the syllable Vaṃ is Ratnasambhava; the syllable Ma is remembered as Tārā; and the syllable Ya is Locanā once again.

The seed-syllable *ka* is the seed-syllable of Māmakī; the seed-syllable *vaṃ* is the seed-syllable of Pāṇḍaravāsinī; the seed-syllable *ma* is the seed-syllable of Tārā; the seed-syllable *ya* is the seed-syllable of Locanā; and again, the seed-syllable *mu* is the seed-syllable of Dhātvīśvarī.
Such is the sequence of the seed-syllables of the four goddesses:
"Locanā is to be known as Maitrī (Loving-kindness), and Māmakī is considered Karuṇā (Compassion)."
Muditā is Pāṇḍaravāsinī; Upekṣā is remembered as Tārā.

Ka is Bharālī; her essential nature (*tatva*) is Locanā. That which is the *āmběk* (the inner core) of compassion (*asiḥ*), not seeking any recompense—that is what is called *maitrī*. Bharālī is Māmakī; her essential nature is Karuṇā. That which is the *āmběk* of suffering, which arises from the pain of all sentient beings (*sarvasattva*) and seeks to liberate them—that is Karuṇā. Bharālī is Pāṇḍaravāsinī; her essential nature is Muditā. That which is the *āmběk* of joy in seeing the joy of all sentient beings—that is Muditā. Bharālī is Tārā; her essential nature is Upekṣā. That which is the *āmběk* of being stainless while rejoicing in the joy of all sentient beings, without perceiving distinctions of joy, nor whether they are performing worship and praise, nor whether they are attaining peace and happiness—without perceiving, without attachment, without aversion, but simply remaining in a state of equanimity, free from grasping (*niṣparigraha*) by nature—that is Upekṣā. This is the essential nature of Bharālī Tārā.

Loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity— these four goddesses are the reality (tattva) of the signless (nirliṅga), O Lord of Yogins. Thus, the supreme samādhi of awakening, which is well-concealed as the secret of all mudrās and Tathāgatas, is to be known by those wise in the conduct of the Buddhas.

[62] What is the essence of *bodhi*, *samādhi*, and the *sarvamudrā* that serves as their characteristic; what is the Tathāgata whom you must honor; and what is the supreme secret of the Tathāgata? It is determined that these are to be realized by him who is wise in the conduct of the Buddhas. What is *mahābodhi*, *samādhi*, the *sarvamudrā*, the mantras, the yoga, and the meditation (*bhāvanā*), as well as the wisdom (*vicakṣaṇa*)—that is the power of the four goddesses: Locanā, Pāṇḍaravāsinī, Māmakī, and Tārā. Thus, the four goddesses are the means of realization; do not be lacking in effort, for they are pure and so is the Lord, the Buddha. For the Lord, the Buddha, cannot be attained unless the power of those four goddesses is attained by that lord of yogins (*yogīśvara*).
Īṃ! This is indeed the essence of the Mahāyāna.
